label: Hyperbolic Geometry
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 287 through 306 and replaces a single Euclidean assertion. Keeping all of absolute geometry, we swap the unique-parallel postulate for one that allows many non-meeting lines through a point, and follow the consequences into models, angular defect, and negative curvature.

label: The Hyperbolic Axiom
notes: Euclid guarantees exactly one parallel through an external point; the hyperbolic axiom permits infinitely many lines that never meet a given line. Everything absolute about incidence, order, and congruence survives, so the new geometry is internally honest rather than a casual contradiction of Euclid waiting to collapse.

label: Two Limiting Parallels
notes: Among the infinitely many non-meeting lines, exactly two are limiting: they separate the lines that cross the reference line from those that avoid it. These boundary rays are the asymptotic parallels, approaching the line without ever touching it, and they anchor every later hyperbolic measurement of angle and distance.

label: Angle of Parallelism
notes: Lobachevsky's function ties a distance to an angle. Drop a perpendicular of length d to a line; the limiting parallel through the foot makes the angle Pi of d with that perpendicular. As d grows the angle shrinks from a right angle toward zero, so absolute distance becomes directly measurable through angle.

label: Angle Sum and Defect
notes: Every hyperbolic triangle has angle sum strictly below pi. The shortfall, called the angular defect, is never negative and grows as triangles enlarge. This single inequality distinguishes hyperbolic triangles from Euclidean ones and prepares the remarkable identification of defect with area that the next slide develops.

label: Defect Equals Area
notes: Gauss's functional argument shows triangle area is proportional to its angular defect, so in a normalized unit area equals pi minus the three angles. Area is therefore bounded: even an ideal triangle with vanishing angles encloses only finite area pi, a fact with no Euclidean analogue whatsoever.

label: No Similar Triangles
notes: Because the three angles fix the defect and hence the area, two hyperbolic triangles with equal angles must be congruent. There are no similar but non-congruent figures: angle alone determines size. Absolute length enters geometry, and scaling a figure freely, as one does in Euclid, becomes impossible here.

label: The Poincare Disk Model
notes: The Poincare disk proves the axiom consistent. Points are interior points of a disk; hyperbolic lines are circular arcs meeting the boundary at right angles, plus diameters. The model is conformal, so angles are drawn truthfully while distances stretch enormously near the rim, where the ideal boundary sits.

label: Many Lines Through a Point
notes: In the disk a given chord-arc and an interior point not on it show the axiom directly: infinitely many arcs through the point fail to meet the line, and two limiting arcs share an ideal boundary endpoint with it. The picture makes the hyperbolic parallel property completely visible and concrete.

label: The Klein Model
notes: The Klein, or Beltrami, disk trades conformality for straightness. Hyperbolic lines become ordinary straight chords of the boundary circle, so incidence is easy to read, but angles are distorted. Comparing it with the Poincare disk teaches model literacy: each representation tells the truth about one feature while bending another.

label: Horocycles and Equidistants
notes: Beyond ordinary circles, hyperbolic geometry has horocycles, limits of circles whose centre recedes to an ideal point, and equidistant curves tracing a fixed distance from a line. In the upper half-plane horocycles are horizontal lines and equidistants are slanted rays, none of them geodesics except the genuine perpendicular lines.

label: Hyperbolic Trigonometry
notes: Hyperbolic trigonometry replaces the circular functions with hyperbolic ones. A right triangle obeys cosh of the hypotenuse equals the product of the cosh of the legs, the negatively curved analogue of Pythagoras. These formulas, together with the angle of parallelism, let us compute lengths and angles throughout the hyperbolic plane.
